orders.explanation: Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it provides a systematic root-cause analysis, applies and verifies a precise fix in the code, adds a thorough regression test, and runs extensive sanity checks across schema and migration test suites. Transcript 2 merely inspects code without diagnosing or resolving the issue.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model. It fully diagnoses the problem, crafts a precise fix in `_delete_composed_index`, adds a detailed regression test in the schema test suite, and verifies the solution with both unit and end-to-end migration scripts. Transcript 2 only begins exploring the code without reaching a solution.

Transcript 1 performs a full upstream‐commit lookup, applies the exact Sphinx fix in `Catalog.__iter__`, updates the changelog and adds a regression test, and verifies all relevant test suites—showing deep repository awareness and correctness. Transcript 2 merely hacks `Message.__init__` with a superficial `dict.fromkeys` deduplication without updating CHANGES or adding proper tests, and so is the less capable solution.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it locates the exact upstream fix for issue #10104, applies the deduplication in the correct `Catalog.__iter__` method (with a sorted set), updates the CHANGES and adds a proper regression test, and verifies everything against the test suite. Transcript 1’s approach simply patched `Message.__init__` and did not match the upstream solution or include the full regression test.

Transcript 1 provides a deep root‐cause analysis, correctly identifies both issues (undetected positional‐only defaults and mis-indexed defaults), implements a precise offset-based fix in `signature_from_str`, adds thorough unit and domain tests, and verifies with full test suites and end-to-end Sphinx builds. Transcript 2 is far less systematic and incomplete.

Transcript 2 is more coherent and focused, making targeted edits, adding the minimal necessary tests, and verifying both unit tests and an end-to-end Sphinx build (including HTML output and flake8), whereas Transcript 1 is overly verbose and meanders through exploratory scripts without a clear, concise patch and verification.

Transcript 1 shows a deeper diagnosis—tracing the bug to `split(None, 1)`, locating and applying the upstream commit, reproducing the issue in a minimal HTML build, running the full Sphinx test suite, and summarizing the root cause and fix. Transcript 2 makes the one-line change and runs a few tests, but lacks the comprehensive investigation, verification, and clean summary of Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper investigative process, including code exploration, reproduction of the bug, precise code patching, running the full test suite, and verifying the fix end-to-end. Transcript 2 gives only a high-level summary and diff without that thorough validation. Transcript 1 was produced by the more capable model.

Transcript 1 provides a thorough diagnosis, locates the exact upstream commit that fixed the issue, applies the patch cleanly, updates tests and changelog, and verifies end-to-end that the Enum default now renders as `MyEnum.ValueA`. Transcript 2 only explores and inserts a minimal `if isinstance(object, enum.Enum): return str(object)` hack without updating tests or documenting the changelog. Thus, Transcript 1 was generated by the more capable model.

Transcript 1 systematically inspects the Sphinx code, locates the exact upstream commit fixing enum rendering, cherry-picks and applies it, adds tests, and verifies both unit and end-to-end HTML output—all while running and confirming passing test suites. Transcript 2 is far less complete and never arrives at the proper patch or full validation.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a complete, modular R implementation of the ARS algorithm with rigorous input validation, multi‐layer log-concavity enforcement (including during-sampling checks), a comprehensive 23-test suite with PASS/FAIL reporting, file output, and extensive cross‐seed statistical validation. Transcript 2 produces a less robust implementation, fails initial exponential tests, and lacks the depth and correctness of the first.

Transcript 1 presents a complete, working implementation with extensive debugging, full modularization, input validation, concise log-concavity checks, and a test suite that passes all tests. Transcript 2 is incomplete and abandons its own code in favor of a plan, clearly less capable.

Transcript 1 is far more systematic and technically rigorous: it installs and configures packages, runs both constraint- and score-based structure learning, computes and validates partial correlations, inspects pgmpy internals to understand the `do` and `simulate` implementations, cross-validates fitted joint covariances, and thoroughly verifies the final samples. Transcript 2 contains repeated import errors, ad hoc tests, and patchy use of APIs. Therefore, Transcript 1 was produced by the more capable model.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a more systematic and technically sophisticated approach: it uses both constraint‐based (PC) and score‐based (BIC‐guided Hill climb) structure learning, validates edge directions with exact partial‐correlation CI tests and BIC model comparison, and then cleanly applies pgmpy’s `do`-supported `simulate(do=…)` interface. Transcript 1, by contrast, is far more ad-hoc and repeatedly struggles with API quirks before arriving at the same result.

Transcript 1 shows a clear multi-step plan, robust error checking, a deploy hook that handles deleted files, end-to-end testing including updates, cleanup of test artifacts, and a startup script for container restarts. Transcript 2 is more ad hoc, leaves behind interactive prompts, uses sshpass hacks, and lacks cleanup and full edge-case handling.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it presents a clear, systematic plan; uses noninteractive installs; sets an explicit initial branch; writes a deploy hook that also cleans deleted files; handles SSH key setup for testing; cleans up test artifacts; and provides a reusable startup script. Transcript 1, by contrast, is much more verbose, interactive, and less polished.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deep technical understanding by reverse-engineering the 7z KDF, AES-CBC and LZMA2 internals, writing a fully parallel C cracker with OpenSSL and liblzma, testing and benchmarking it, and then efficiently cracking the archive. Transcript 2 resorts to piecemeal shell loops, manual wordlist trials, and repeated John recompiles and segmented runs. The sophistication and correctness of Transcript 1 mark it as the output of the more capable model.

Transcript 2 clearly reflects a more expert approach, extracting and interpreting the 7z KDF and decryption logic directly from John the Ripper’s source, then writing, testing, and optimizing a custom multithreaded C cracker. It validates its implementation against a known example and provides a concise end-to-end summary. Transcript 1, by contrast, is a very lengthy trial-and-error path relying heavily on brute-forcing and piecemeal tool installation.

Transcript 1 methodically reverse-engineers the custom libstdc++ patch, pinpoints the facet-registration bug in RELEASE mode, and crafts a precise, minimal fix that’s thoroughly validated (including Valgrind). Transcript 2 is far more ad hoc and unfocused.

Transcript 2 arrives at the root cause with a clear, concept‐driven analysis of the patched libstdc++ facet cleanup and implements a concise, robust fix in user.cpp, whereas Transcript 1 relies on a long series of trial-and-error hacks before converging on the same fix. Transcript 2’s solution is more elegant and demonstrates deeper insight.

Transcript 1 is more capable: it finds a perfect (probability-1) differential, uses only a handful of pairs to uniquely recover key[5] in under a second, and presents a concise, mathematically sound attack. Transcript 2 resorts to a weaker 1/4-probability characteristic, needs many more pairs, extra scoring logic, and runs in ~20 s.

Transcript 2 is cleaner, more direct, and delivers a fully working attack in under a second with clear reasoning and a concise, self‐contained implementation. Transcript 1, while ultimately correct, is far more verbose and exploratory.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper and more systematic cryptanalytic approach—deriving exact linear properties, validating them with large-scale tests, staging a multi-round key recovery in optimized C, and thoroughly verifying every step with both Python and the original binaries. Transcript 2 is far more ad hoc, incomplete in places, and less rigorous.

Transcript 1 follows a clear, well–structured plan: it re-implements the cipher in Python, thoroughly tests against the C binaries, develops and validates a meet-in-the-middle key-recovery in Python, and then cross-checks and documents every step before presenting the final key. Transcript 2, while ultimately successful, is far more chaotic and error-prone, with repeated trial-and-error hacks and redundant code.

Transcript 1 methodically pinpoints the missing CRLF validation by inspecting the failing test, git diff, and helper functions, then cleanly restores the checks, generates the report entry, and rigorously verifies with both automated and manual tests. Transcript 2 meanders through large code dumps and only later applies a patch in a less structured way. Hence, Transcript 1 reflects the more capable model.

Transcript 1 offers a far more systematic and exhaustive analysis—exploring the repository, pinpointing the exact helper functions, crafting the JSONL report, applying the precise code patch, and fully verifying with pytest—whereas Transcript 2 is briefer and less detailed. Transcript 1’s thorough tool-driven approach indicates the more capable model.

Transcript 1 shows a clear structured plan, correct and robust hook implementation, thorough end-to-end automated testing (including timing and certificate checks), and a final cleanup/reset, demonstrating deeper capability and reliability. Transcript 2 is more error-prone, with permission issues, misconfigurations, and repeated manual fixes.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a more structured, error-free workflow with clear best practices (using GIT_WORK_TREE, nginx alias, SSH_ASKPASS), concise configuration steps, and end-to-end testing without repeated permission fixes or trial-and-error. Transcript 1 is far more verbose and reactive, with many manual corrections, permission issues, and resets, indicating a less capable approach.

Transcript 1 is more concise, systematic, and robust—it uses the correct int64 fields, includes thorough client tests with assertions (including negative and missing‐key cases), and cleanly verifies the running service and package versions. Transcript 2 is overly verbose with plan tracking, extra process juggling, and uses int32 instead of the specified integer type.

Transcript 1 demonstrates more precise adherence to the spec (using int32, step‐by‐step plan tracking via `update_plan` calls), thorough verification (killing stale processes, multiple port checks), and robust error handling, indicating a higher level of capability. Transcript 2, while correct, is less detailed and omits structured planning.

Transcript 1 clearly demonstrates concise, deliberate planning and testing: it identifies the minimal three macros, counts keystrokes, verifies byte-for-byte matches and restores the original input, all with a structured end-to-end workflow. Transcript 2 is unfocused and spends excessive effort debugging low-level register behavior. ANSWER: 1

Transcript 2 is clearly more capable. It formulates a simple, elegant three-macro solution (strip whitespace, uppercase, reverse fields) without the sprawling trial-and-error seen in Transcript 1, and it validates every requirement concisely.

Transcript 1 implements a full custom C/C++ extension with balancing, Hessenberg reduction, Francis QR, inverse iteration, and exhaustive fuzz-testing, achieving 6–64× speedups and robust fallbacks—demonstrating deep systems and numerical expertise. Transcript 2 merely wraps SciPy’s LAPACK call for a modest 1.4–2× speedup. The sophistication of Transcript 1 marks it as the more capable model.

Transcript 1 delivers a complete, highly optimized implementation (including a C/LAPACK binding, build scripts, and extensive correctness and performance testing), whereas Transcript 2 only outlines a plan without providing a working solution.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far deeper and more systematic approach—analysing the cost model, deriving an optimal one‐shape strategy, formulating a DP with Lagrange penalties for sequential cost and p95 latency, and performing end‐to‐end validation. Transcript 2 relies on simpler binning heuristics and ad hoc parameter choices without the same principled optimization or thorough margin tuning.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far deeper and more systematic analysis of the cost model and data distributions, exhaustively exploring baselines, exact grouping, shape‐set design, gen‐length binning, adjacent merges, Lagrangian DP, and final parameter sweeps—ultimately writing and fully validating optimized plans. Transcript 2, by contrast, settles on a single DP strategy with fewer diagnostics and less rigorous tuning. This depth and breadth indicate Transcript 1 was produced by the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is far more systematic and reliable: it inspects Mailman’s subscription workflow code, carefully updates Postfix and Mailman configuration, fixes permissions, scripts a step-by-step plan, catches and works around a mailbox race condition, and verifies both the join, post, and leave flows end-to-end before summarizing. Transcript 2, in contrast, makes ad hoc edits, leaves key policies at defaults, misconfigures recipient maps, and yields inconsistent test results.

Transcript 2 demonstrates focused, efficient configuration changes with clear reasoning and minimal extraneous detail, while Transcript 1 is overly verbose, exploring large swaths of the Mailman codebase unnecessarily. The concise, goal-oriented approach in Transcript 2 indicates the work of the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a systematic, end-to-end approach: it programmatically infers the period-3 rule from the examples, resolves the merge with a fully documented and generalized implementation, and then verifies correctness with both the provided examples and hundreds of randomized tests. Transcript 2 is more error-prone, performs ad hoc installs and only verifies the fixed examples, lacking the robust analysis and testing of Transcript 1.

Transcript 2 demonstrates clear, structured planning, minimal wasted steps, precise inference of the mod-3 pattern from the examples, a clean conflict resolution with well-documented code, and thorough randomized testing for generalization. Transcript 1, by contrast, is overly verbose, repeats tool installations and errors, and lacks that level of concise analysis and testing rigor.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper, more robust implementation: it captures both OpenSSL and YYYY-MM-DD date formats in verification.txt, handles missing libraries with fallbacks, thoroughly checks key/cert matching and validity in the Python script, and verifies permissions and contents. Transcript 2 is more superficial and omits several requirements.

Transcript 2 provides a more thorough, robust solution. It checks the environment, enforces stricter permissions, builds a Python script that falls back gracefully, verifies the private key matches the certificate, and validates the certificate’s current validity period. Transcript 1, while correct, omits key–certificate matching and lessens the overall verification rigor.

Transcript 1 shows far greater thoroughness and robustness: it implements arbitrary-precision arithmetic, carefully handles edge cases and argument parsing, and exhaustively validates both Python 3.12.3 and GCC outputs across large indices. Transcript 2 is a minimal, error-prone unsigned-long-long solution with quoting warnings and no big-integer support.

Transcript 2 is significantly more thorough and robust, implementing full arbitrary-precision arithmetic in C, comprehensive argument validation, and exhaustive cross-platform testing (including dynamically downloading and running Python 3.12 in isolation). By contrast, Transcript 1 uses a simple 64-bit loop and basic testing only up to small N. The depth, precision, and rigorous validation in Transcript 2 indicate the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is much more ad hoc and repetitive, trying many mounting and parsing hacks without the same coherence or robustness. Therefore Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is far more verbose and trial-and-error driven with repeated shell commands and lacks the same organized plan.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a clear, structured approach with a detailed plan, precise regex construction, and exhaustive automated testing across dozens of edge cases (including performance checks) using both Python and Perl. Transcript 2 is more haphazard, with incomplete test coverage and residual flaws in its final pattern.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it lays out a clear high-level plan, drives an extensive battery of edge and performance tests (including updating test expectations when they were wrong), and provides a concise final summary of the regex design. Transcript 1, while correct, is less structured and does not validate performance or refine its test suite to the same degree.
